# Cap retrieval output in summary search: inline Why/Fix length, hit budget, common-token downrank

`search` summary mode is small for KNOWLEDGE/RULE but still bloats on NEGATIVE/ERROR and on low-value matches. A sohot session's `search("sweep-check")` and `search("deploy guard")` each returned ~20 hits, including the same 6-7 irrelevant NEGATIVEs (#1,#3,#8,#10,#11,#14,#16) matched only on a common token ("check"/"sweep"/"deploy"/"testing"), each inlining its full (and currently polluted) Why/Fix. Even post-sanitize (#170) the Why/Fix is multi-paragraph; a one-line hit is cheap, seven 2 KB inlined bodies are not.

## Fix (search.py)
1. Cap the inline NEGATIVE Why/Fix and ERROR root_cause/fix in summary mode at a few hundred chars each, with a "… (get_entry for full)" pointer. `detail="full"` stays uncapped.
2. Cap total hits returned per query. The public `search` default `limit` is 10 per entity type → up to 40 + related. Add an overall response ceiling (~8-10 hits) independent of per-scope limit.
3. Downrank or drop a hit whose only match is a single common token: when a NEGATIVE/ERROR matches on a token that is also a stopword-ish high-frequency term and nothing more distinctive, it should not outrank or crowd out a real RULE hit. Simplest: a relevance floor for NEGATIVE/ERROR in the multi-scope "all" path so generic single-token matches drop below the fold.

## Acceptance
- `search("deploy guard")` and `search("sweep-check")` each return under ~3 KB, with RULE #756 and #868 still present for "deploy guard".
- `detail="full"` is unchanged (still returns whole bodies).

# #137a: server-owned per-session topic-coverage ledger + compaction reconciliation

Child of #137 (retrieval scheduling umbrella). **The foundation — the other layers depend on this.**

Give mcm-engine a lightweight **server-owned, per-FastMCP-session** retrieval ledger: coverage by *topic* (not TTL), each entry carrying `{topic, searched_at, query, result_ids, resident}`. Only the server sees the query + result ids, so the server owns it; the PreToolUse hook (a separate process) reads shared state or asks the server.

Critical requirement — **coverage is not context residency** (KB CONTEXT #3, the founding anti-amnesia concern): a ledger that says "topic covered" after the retrieved bodies were summarized out of context recreates the exact failure mcm-engine exists to defeat. So carry a `resident` flag distinct from `searched_at`, and **reconcile it at the compaction boundary** — on `PreCompact`/`PostCompact` and `SessionStart`, mark prior coverage non-resident (or re-surface it). A non-resident topic does not satisfy enforcement.

Keyed per FastMCP session (RULE #116 / ScopedTracker), same as the existing tracker state.

### Acceptance
- Server-owned, per-session, per-topic coverage ledger with a `resident` flag.
- `search` (and report_error auto-search) record coverage: topic, query, result_ids, searched_at, resident=true.
- Reconciled at PreCompact/PostCompact/SessionStart (resident flips false on compaction).
- Unit tests for record + reconcile; no behavior change to enforcement yet (that's the PreToolUse child).

# search summary mode should carry a match snippet (keep 'why it matched' under semantic/non-FTS5 backends)

## Problem

#119 made `search` default to compact summary hits (id, kind, title/topic, one-line summary, tags) and defer bodies to `get_entry`. That progressive-disclosure win rests on an implicit assumption: the agent can judge a hit's relevance *from the summary line* and only fetch the bodies worth paying for.

That assumption holds under **lexical** search (SQLite FTS5, Postgres FTS), where the query token is literally in the matched text, so the agent knows why a hit came back. It weakens under a **semantic/vector** backend (the direction the live server + lodestone are moving — FTS5 is being retired): a hit can match on meaning the summary line never surfaces, so the agent can't tell from the one-liner whether the body is relevant. Result: either wasted `get_entry` round-trips on bad hits, or wrongly skipping a good hit. No wrong results, but the ergonomics of summary-first degrade exactly where we're headed.

## Root cause

`detail`/summary rendering (`tools/search.py`) is fully decoupled from the search backend (good — see `_scope_block`), but `SearchHit` (`backends/__init__.py:323`) carries `entity_type / entity_id / score / is_pinned / is_stale / counters_snapshot / row` and **no matched-text field**. The "why it matched" signal every backend computes internally is thrown away before rendering.

## Proposal

Add an optional `snippet: Optional[str] = None` to `SearchHit`. Each adapter populates it from the highlight it already produces; summary-mode rendering appends it under the one-liner when present. Adapters that can't produce one leave it `None` and rendering falls back to today's behavior — no regression, no required work for any adapter.

Per-adapter source of the snippet:
- **SQLite FTS5**: `snippet()` / `highlight()` aux functions.
- **Postgres**: `ts_headline()` over the indexed document.
- **OpenSearch**: the `highlight` block already in the response.
- **Semantic/vector backend (future)**: the matched chunk/passage it ranked on — this is the case the issue exists for.

Summary rendering: append a short, length-capped snippet line to each hit in `detail="summary"`. `detail="full"` is unchanged (it already has the whole body). Keep the once-per-response `get_entry` footer.

## Acceptance
- `SearchHit.snippet` optional, defaults `None`; omitting it is valid for any adapter.
- At least the lexical adapters (SQLite, Postgres) populate it; summary hits render it when present.
- Snippet length is bounded (config, e.g. `MCM_SNIPPET_MAX`) so this doesn't reintroduce the token bloat #119 removed.
- Conformance covers: snippet present renders; snippet `None` renders exactly as today.

## Non-goals
- Not changing matching, ranking, or `include_archived`.
- Not changing the summary-vs-full default.
- Not building the semantic backend here — only making sure summary mode can carry its match signal when it lands.

Follow-up to #119.

# search summary mode must keep Why/Fix inline for NEGATIVE (and ERROR) hits

## Problem

#119 strips the body from a hit in `detail="summary"` (the default). For ordinary knowledge that only makes a hit *incomplete* — worst case you `get_entry` it. For **negative knowledge** it is a correctness bug, because the body **is** the payload and the failure mode is asymmetric.

`tools/search.py:272` renders a NEGATIVE summary hit as just:

    [NEGATIVE #id] <category>: <what_failed>

`Why` (`why_failed`) and `Fix` (`correct_approach`) are gated behind `detail == "full"` (lines 273-277). So a plain `search` tells the agent *that* an approach failed but hides *why it must stay rejected* and *what to do instead*. The agent can then re-attempt the dead end, or be unable to tell whether its current plan is the rejected one — the exact outcome the anti-pattern store exists to prevent. ERROR hits have the same shape: `root_cause` / `fix` are gated at `tools/search.py:296`.

Note #122 only restored full bodies for the `report_error` auto-search path. A direct `search(scope="negative")` (or an all-scope search that surfaces a negative) still strips Why/Fix.

## Why this is the right asymmetry

The #119 token win comes from not carrying large *knowledge* bodies. Negative/error bodies are short (a Why line + a Fix line), so keeping them inline barely dents the win, and their whole value is being seen at the moment of the hit, not one `get_entry` later.

## Proposal

In summary mode, keep `Why`/`Fix` inline for NEGATIVE hits and `root_cause`/`fix` for ERROR hits. Knowledge stays summary-only (its bodies are the token problem). Optionally cap each field's length (reuse whatever `MCM_SNIPPET_MAX`-style bound #135 lands) so a pathologically long negative can't reintroduce bloat.

## Acceptance
- `search` (summary, default) renders Why + Fix for a NEGATIVE hit and root cause + fix for an ERROR hit.
- Knowledge summary rendering unchanged.
- Conformance: a negative/error hit in summary mode contains its Why/Fix (root cause/fix); a knowledge hit in summary mode still omits its body.

Follow-up to #119 / #122. Distinct from #135 (which adds a match *snippet*); this is about which structured fields summary mode keeps per kind.

# get_last_session returns the global latest handoff — no per-caller/workspace scoping, so shared deployments resume the wrong session

## Summary

On any deployment where more than one working context shares a single mcm-engine store (multiple users behind one server, or one user across several projects), `session_start` and `get_resume_context` routinely surface a handoff belonging to a *different* context. The user asks to resume project A and is handed project B's handoff.

## Root cause

`get_last_session` is unscoped in both adapters:

```python
# adapters/sqlite/storage.py
"SELECT * FROM sessions ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
# adapters/postgres/storage.py — identical
```

It returns the single newest row across the entire `sessions` table. There is only ever one candidate, so "resume" can't pick correctly — it picks globally-latest.

Contributing facts:
- The `sessions` table (`schema.py`) has **no scoping column** — no project, no owner/principal — unlike `knowledge`/`negative_knowledge`/`errors`, which all carry `project` (and project indexes).
- `session_handoff` accepts only `status/current_task/next_steps/blockers` — the client cannot tag a handoff with any scope key at write time.
- `get_last_session(*, caller=None)` already has a **vestigial `caller` param that is never populated or used** for filtering.
- Both `session_start` (the "Last handoff" block) and `get_resume_context` call `get_last_session()` with no argument.

## Why `project_name` alone doesn't fix it

`MCM_PROJECT_NAME` is a **server-global** config value — every request through one server carries the same project. Adding a `project` column keyed to `MCM_PROJECT_NAME` would sort every caller into the same bucket and change nothing for the common "one shared server" topology. It also wouldn't separate a single user's multiple projects.

The scoping key has to be **per-request**, not per-server.

## What's already available

`principal.py` exposes `get_transport_principal()` — the bearer-token identity for the in-flight request, carried in a ContextVar and already used as the fallback in `resolve_actor()`. So an authenticated per-caller identity is reachable from any tool call today; the session tools simply don't consult it.

## Proposed fix

1. **Schema:** add scoping columns to `sessions` — at minimum `principal TEXT` (who), and an optional client-supplied `workspace TEXT` label (what — so one principal working on N projects stays separated). Additive migration + index, mirroring the `project` columns on the other tables.
2. **Write:** `session_handoff` stamps the current transport principal automatically, and accepts an optional `workspace` argument (or derives one — see open question) so the row is self-describing.
3. **Read:** `get_last_session(*, principal=None, workspace=None)` → `WHERE` on the provided keys, `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`. `session_start` / `get_resume_context` pass the in-flight principal (+ workspace when known).
4. **Back-compat:** pre-migration rows have NULL scope. Treat a NULL-scope handoff as a **clearly-labeled global fallback**, shown only when no scoped row matches, so existing handoffs aren't orphaned.

## Open question for maintainer

What should `workspace` derive from when the client doesn't pass one? Options: (a) principal-only scoping (simplest, but conflates one user's multiple projects); (b) an explicit client-supplied label on `session_handoff`/`session_start`; (c) something the client already sends (e.g. a cwd/repo hint). Leaning (b) with (a) as the fallback, but the right default depends on how you want stdio/unauthenticated contexts (principal = None) to behave — today they'd all collapse to the NULL bucket.

## Impact

Silent and confusing: the agent confidently narrates the wrong project's state as if it were the current one, and a user who trusts it can act on stale/irrelevant context. Severity scales with the number of concurrent contexts sharing the store.

# stdio startup sync failure is invisible to the client: server reports ready and serves a stale index

In stdio mode, a failed startup sync is invisible to the client. The server comes up, reports ready, and serves a stale index — searches then return confident "no results" for rules that exist on disk and are committed.

`server.py` `run()` catches it and moves on:

```python
try:
    counts = self.watcher.sync_once()
    log(f"sync_rules at stdio startup: {counts}")
except Exception as e:
    log(f"sync_rules at stdio startup failed (non-fatal): {e}")
self.mcp.run()
```

The log line is real and lands in `log_path`, but `log()` writes to file only and deliberately never touches stderr ("MCP clients treat stderr as failure"). Nothing reaches the client, and no tool response carries a staleness signal, so neither the agent nor the user has any way to learn the index is behind the files.

Observed twice on a single-user laptop, 2026-07-28 and again 2026-08-08 (v3.8.0, SQLite, `source_of_truth=files`). Six stdio servers alive against one `--project-root`, oldest 12 days; one held a write transaction, so every new server's startup sync failed:

```
[2026-08-08 20:55:10] sync_rules at stdio startup failed (non-fatal): database is locked
```

Two committed rules never reached the cache — 35 rows against 37 `rules/*.md`. Searches for them returned nothing, with no error anywhere in the session. The corroborating symptom is a WAL that has not checkpointed: `knowledge.db-wal` at 2.3 MB against a 278 KB `knowledge.db`.

Widening `busy_timeout` from the hardcoded 5s (`db.py:145`) to four minutes still blocked indefinitely, so the retry path cannot recover from a genuinely held transaction — the cross-process case is not the intra-process contention fixed in #79/#83. That contention is arguably working as designed for a laptop running many sessions; the defect is that its outcome is unobservable.

Some options, roughly increasing in cost:

- Record the failure in server state and prefix affected `search` / `session_start` responses with a staleness warning, so the agent sees it at the point of use.
- Expose last-sync status (timestamp, counts, last error) as a tool or resource for explicit checks.
- Retry the startup sync in the background rather than once at boot, so a transient holder resolves itself.
- Return a non-fatal notice through the MCP client's logging channel, which is not stderr and is safe to use.

Happy to send a PR for the first if that's the direction you'd want.

# --allowed-host / MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS ignored by streamable-http transport (421 on permitted Host)

# `--allowed-host` / `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is ignored by the streamable-http transport (server 421s a permitted Host)

## Summary
When `mcm-engine serve --transport streamable-http` runs behind a reverse proxy / ingress, requests whose `Host` header is a configured allowed host are still rejected with **HTTP 421 "Invalid Host header"**. The allow-list (`--allowed-host` / `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS`) has no effect for streamable-http; only the localhost defaults (`127.0.0.1:*`, `localhost:*`, `[::1]:*`) are enforced.

## Environment
- mcm-engine 3.5.0 (also present on current `main`: `transport.py`).
- Transport: `streamable-http`, bound `--host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080`.
- Reached via an internal AWS ALB at `https://mcm.internal.example` (Host = that FQDN).

## Repro
1. `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS=example.internal mcm-engine serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --transport streamable-http`
2. `curl -H 'Host: example.internal' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid>' \
   -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
   -X POST http://<addr>:8080/mcp -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}'`
3. → `421 Invalid Host header` (bearer auth passes first — an unauthenticated call 401s — so this is specifically Host validation, after auth).

Confirmed the env is read and passed: `cmd_serve` reads `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS` and calls `serve(..., allowed_hosts=...)`, and `_configure_transport_security` builds the expected pattern (`example.internal:*` via `_host_pattern`). Yet a live server still shows only the localhost allow-list enforcing.

## Root cause (ordering)
In `transport.py serve()`:
```python
_configure_transport_security(server, host=host, allowed_hosts=allowed_hosts, enable=...)  # mutates server.mcp.settings.transport_security
app = build_asgi_app(server, transport=transport)  # -> server.mcp.streamable_http_app()
```
`_configure_transport_security` mutates `server.mcp.settings.transport_security` **after** FastMCP is constructed, but `streamable_http_app()` builds its DNS-rebinding middleware from FastMCP's own (localhost-only) transport-security at app-build time and does not honor the post-construction mutation. So the alignment is discarded and the localhost-only list is what actually enforces. (A freshly built `MCMServer` shows `allowed_hosts=['127.0.0.1:*','localhost:*','[::1]:*']`.)

## Suggested fix
Configure FastMCP's `TransportSecuritySettings` **before** the transport app is built — e.g. construct `FastMCP` with the settings up front, or set them via whatever `streamable_http_app()` reads at build time — so `--allowed-host` takes effect for streamable-http (it may already work for `sse`; worth confirming both). Add a regression test: build the streamable-http app with an allow-list and assert a request with that Host is accepted.

## Workaround in use
Setting `MCM_DNS_REBINDING_PROTECTION=0` disables Host validation entirely and unblocks ingress access. Acceptable only on a trusted, non-browser endpoint (internal LB, private DNS) and does **not** weaken bearer auth. Not a fix — the allow-list should work.

# search blocks ~20s on SQLite lock from post-search counter bumps

# `search` blocks ~20 seconds on SQLite lock from post-search counter bumps

**Version:** 2.0.0

I've started working this into my homelab setup piece (project) by piece. I think I've hit a performance issue and wanted to share what I found in case it's useful.

## Symptom

Every `search` call takes ~15–30 seconds; longer queries exceed a 30 sec. client timeout and return nothing. Reproduces on a single idle `mcm-engine run` (stdio) against its own copy of a small (27-rule) tree with no external concurrency. Timing is deterministic (~20.9 s for the same 3-term query), so it doesn't look like network or model-load.

## What I found

The search itself is fine; the stall is a SQLite lock wait, not work:

- `sample <pid>` mid-call is 100% in `sqlite3_step → unixSleep → nanosleep` (the `busy_timeout` back-off).
- Calling the read-only adapter directly: `SqliteSearch.search(...)` returns in **0.4 ms**.
- The time is in the post-search `hit_count` / `last_hit_at` bumps in `_scope_block` (tools/search.py:243-254) — up to ~2 writes × limit × 2 scopes per call.
- Those writes appear to self-contend across the embedded adapters' separate connections to the same file (db.py:117-132, `busy_timeout=5000`). Reproduced in isolation: two connections / one file, second writer blocks **5262 ms** then `database is locked`. A few of those per search ≈ the ~20 s observed.

The `try/except` around `counters.increment` (search.py:248-253) swallows the resulting exception so results still return, but the 5 s sleep happens before the exception is raised.

## Possible directions (whatever fits best)

1. Lower `busy_timeout` (e.g. ~250 ms) for the bump path. This bounds the worst case to ~1 s.
2. Run the best-effort bumps on the same connection that served the read, or off the request path.
3. A single shared writer connection for the embedded adapters.

Happy to open a PR or provide more detail (sample output, repro script) if that would help.

# Rule-like gate rejects descriptive architectural facts (normative-word requirement too strict for ingest)

## Summary

`is_rule_like` (`src/mcm_engine/ingest/rulesift.py`) requires a **normative/warning marker** (`must|never|always|avoid|ensure|require|note|warning|gotcha|…`) for a span to survive the funnel. This drops **descriptive architectural facts** that are genuinely rule-worthy knowledge but phrased declaratively rather than as an imperative.

## Repro

Ingesting `DoddE/stork` (a real Terraform artifact-repository project) via `ingest --remote`:

```
# funnel:   19 raw candidates -> 0 rule-like span(s)
```

All 19 candidates were dropped. The README describes a real "dirty/clean" artifact-promotion architecture (AWS CodeArtifact intake→scan→clean, Harbor+Trivy, EventBridge-triggered promotion, internal ALB) — high-value KB content — but contains no `must`/`never`/`note`/`gotcha`, so `is_rule_like` returns `False` for every span.

## Root cause

`is_rule_like` (rulesift.py:140):

```python
def is_rule_like(text: str) -> bool:
    if len(dedup.normalize(text).split()) < MIN_TOKENS:
        return False
    return _NORMATIVE_RE.search(text) is not None   # <-- requires a normative marker
```

`_NORMATIVE_RE` is deliberately tight (comment: "over-admitting here just means more spans reach the future model stage, but for Slice 1 the agent eyeballs survivors, so we keep the gate tight").

Note this gate runs in **two** places and both must agree:
- client-side in `extract`/funnel (`sift`)
- **server-side** in `sift_spans` (rulesift.py) behind the `sift_candidates` MCP tool

So a client can't bypass it alone — `sift_candidates` re-applies `is_rule_like`.

## Impact

Now that there's a curation/adjudication stage downstream (e.g. an LLM adjudicator deciding keep/skip on survivors — see the platform's `gitlab_ingest.py` flow), the tight normative gate is the wrong place to enforce precision. It silently discards descriptive architecture, contracts, and conventions before anything smarter can judge them. The "Slice 1 agent eyeballs survivors" assumption no longer holds for automated ingest.

## Proposed fix (options)

1. **Broaden `is_rule_like`** to admit descriptive-but-substantive spans: markdown headings + prose, "X provides/creates/uses Y" declaratives, tables, module/contract descriptions — while still dropping trivially short spans and pure API-doc boilerplate (`Args:`/`Returns:`).
2. **Add a `gate=` / `strict=` parameter** to `sift_spans` (and expose it on the `sift_candidates` tool) so callers can opt into "band everything, let the caller/adjudicator decide" while keeping MinHash novelty banding + intra-run dedup. Backward-compatible default = current strict behavior.
3. Combination: keep a *minimum-substance* floor (token count, not just `MIN_TOKENS=3`; reject nav/boilerplate) but drop the hard normative-marker requirement when `gate=False`.

Option 2 is the least disruptive and unblocks automated descriptive-content ingest without changing default behavior for existing callers.

## Acceptance

- `ingest --remote` on a descriptive repo like stork yields non-zero rule-like spans (via the new mode/broadened gate).
- Existing strict behavior remains the default (no regression for curated rule ingest).
- Both client `sift` and server `sift_spans`/`sift_candidates` honor the same setting.

# link_knowledge requires entry ids that no tool surfaces, and its escalated nudge hard-blocks discovery (deadlock)

## Summary

`link_knowledge` requires integer entry ids (`source_id`, `target_id`), but **no tool surfaces those ids** — `search` and `kb_recall` render titles + bodies, never the row id. So a caller cannot know what to pass.

This compounds into a **deadlock**: the periodic-nudge system escalates an ignored `link_knowledge` nudge into a **hard block that forbids *all* other tools — including `search`** — until `link_knowledge` is called. In that state you must call `link_knowledge` but cannot look up the ids to pass it, forcing a blind guess (which creates wrong edges — the exact opposite of what the relations graph is for) or repeated errors.

## Repro (hit live)

1. Store several knowledge entries over a session without calling `link_knowledge`.
2. The nudge escalates: every tool call is rejected with `ESCALATED BLOCK: 'periodic:link_knowledge' ... You MUST call link_knowledge before any other tool.`
3. Try to discover ids to link → `search` is also blocked.
4. Only option left: guess ids by insertion order (I guessed knowledge `12 -> 10`). Guess is unverifiable and likely wrong.

## Why it's bad

- The feature is unusable as designed: you can't build correct edges without ids you can't obtain.
- The escalation actively drives *garbage* edges (blind guesses), polluting the very graph `get_related` traverses.
- Blocking the read tool needed to satisfy the nudge is a self-defeating gate.

## Fix options (pick one or more)

1. **Surface entry ids in `search` / `kb_recall` output.** Cheapest; makes correct linking possible at all. (Probably necessary regardless of the others.)
2. **Let `link_knowledge` resolve by title/slug** in addition to integer id.
3. **Don't put id-requiring tools in the hard-block set** — keep `link_knowledge` advisory, or guarantee at least one read tool (`search`) stays usable while blocked so the nudge is satisfiable.
4. **Nudge system invariant:** never escalate-to-block a tool whose required inputs cannot be obtained from the blocked state.

## Relevant code

- `src/mcm_engine/tools/relations.py` — `link_knowledge`
- `src/mcm_engine/tools/search.py` — `search` result rendering (add ids)
- `src/mcm_engine/tracker.py` + `mcm-engine.yaml` (`nudges.periodic_tools`, `nudge_escalation_threshold`) — escalation/blocking

Found while dogfooding the mcm KB during the ingest-funnel work.
